_meta.title: Στοά — the heads of the Stoic school in Athens, c. 300 – 109 BCE
_meta.note: The seven heads of the Stoa from Zeno of Citium to Panaetius, numbered by succession, plotted at birthplace. After Panaetius (109 BCE) the single Athenian succession breaks; 'later' figures are Stoic leaders active afterward whom no clean head-list covers.
_meta.sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives, Book 7; Cicero, Academica and De oratore; Smith, Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

heads.name: Zeno of Citium
heads.bio: Founder of Stoicism. A merchant from Citium who, after a shipwreck brought him to Athens, turned to philosophy and taught in the painted colonnade (Stoa Poikile) that gave the school its name. He built an ethics of living in accord with nature and reason.

heads.name: Cleanthes
heads.bio: Zeno's devoted successor, a former boxer who worked nights drawing water to study by day. His Hymn to Zeus is the fullest surviving Stoic religious poem, casting the cosmos as governed by a rational, providential god.

heads.name: Chrysippus
heads.bio: The 'second founder' of Stoicism, who systematized its logic, physics, and ethics so thoroughly that it was said 'without Chrysippus there would be no Stoa.' He wrote over seven hundred books and founded propositional logic.
heads.note: Born at Soli; his father was from Tarsus.

heads.name: Zeno of Tarsus
heads.bio: Chrysippus' pupil and successor, remembered as cautious in doctrine — he is said to have doubted the Stoic teaching that the cosmos periodically dissolves in fire.

heads.name: Diogenes of Babylon
heads.bio: Called 'of Babylon' though born at Seleucia on the Tigris. He carried Stoicism to Rome on the famous philosophers' embassy of 155 BCE and wrote influentially on language, music, and ethics.
heads.note: Called 'of Babylon,' he was born at Seleucia on the Tigris.

heads.name: Antipater of Tarsus
heads.bio: Successor of Diogenes and teacher of Panaetius. He defended Stoic logic against the skeptical Academy of Carneades and refined Stoic ethics on the duties of everyday life.

heads.name: Panaetius
heads.bio: The last undisputed head of the Athenian Stoa, who softened its austerity and brought it to the Roman elite — his work on moral duty underlies Cicero's De Officiis. After him the Athenian succession fractured.

later.name: Mnesarchus
later.headship: fl. c. 95 BCE · later Stoic leader
later.bio: Named by Cicero as one of the leaders of the Stoics at Athens around 95 BCE, after the single succession had broken apart.

later.name: Dardanus
later.headship: fl. c. 95 BCE · later Stoic leader
later.bio: Named by Cicero alongside Mnesarchus as a leading Athenian Stoic of the late second century BCE, when the school no longer had one clear head.

later.name: Posidonius
later.bio: Panaetius' pupil and the most wide-ranging Stoic of all — philosopher, historian, astronomer, geographer. He ran his own celebrated school on Rhodes rather than heading the Athenian Stoa.
